item.title: Defending Pure Authorship Is Disloyalty to History
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
Defending Pure Authorship Is Disloyalty to History

Defending pure authorship is a disloyalty to history. It is a disloyalty because it rests upon a fiction: that the author creates alone, from within himself, something that did not belong to anyone before. The history of culture refutes this fiction on every page. And AI, by performing recombination at an unprecedented scale, is not introducing something new. It is merely making visible what has always been before us: the collective, ancestral, imitative, technical, and accumulative dimension of what we have always called creation.

To say that a piece of music was “made by AI” is, in this sense, a technical reductionism, not a sufficient conceptual description. It may indicate that the immediate generation was executed by a model. But it becomes misleading when it suggests that AI created something by itself, as an originating subject external to humanity. There is no AI process today that does not have, at minimum, a human origin: someone conceived the architecture, established objectives, chose data, built infrastructure, financed the project, configured the system, gave an order, or instituted the process that will trigger it. Even when the generation seems automatic, there is a prior human decision that created the conditions for automation.

AI is not a rival culture. It is a human technique for reorganizing the human stock. This technique is already altering cultural production. In music, Deezer reported that it went from approximately ten thousand fully AI-generated tracks received per day in January 2025 to about ninety thousand at the peak of June 2026 — more than half of the platform’s daily new uploads. In publishing, studies on independent fiction on Amazon record an explosive catalog growth in the period following the spread of generative models. These numbers are often presented as proof of an invasion. I read them differently: they show that humanity has found a new instrument for reorganizing its cultural heritage at an unprecedented scale.

And this instrument does more than increase the volume of content. It reduces barriers. People who did not know how to play instruments, record, produce, edit, translate, lay out, illustrate, or structure a text can now transform an idea into a publishable song or book. Self-publishing already existed, digital distribution already existed. But AI makes viable, for far more people, the passage between having something to say and being able to give public form to that something.

This text is the sixth of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.

item.title: Ourselves
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
Ourselves

In culture, the reaction is more intense because we still imagine art as the last inviolable territory. When a machine reorganizes language, images, and sounds convincingly, it does not only threaten jobs. It threatens the fiction that the author creates alone, from within himself, something that did not belong to anyone. I do not believe in that fiction.

Creativity is not the production of the without-antecedent. It is the actualization of possibilities within a heritage that exceeds us. A work is not less human because it was mediated by algorithm. It is human because it only exists within the long human chain that produced its elements, its instruments, its circulation, and its meanings.

There is no alien in the human cultural cauldron. There is humanity producing increasingly powerful tools to reorganize its own heritage. The challenge is not to defend an imaginary purity of human creation against a foreign intelligence. The challenge is to prevent a small portion of humanity from capturing the common stock, controlling the tools of cultural reorganization, and transforming a collective heritage into a private monopoly.

The asymmetry of credit has always existed. The difference is that now we have instruments that force us to see it. And, once we see it, we can no longer pretend that creation is a solitary, originary act, disconnected from the stock that made it possible.

The question is not whether AI will replace artists. The question is whether we will continue to believe the story artists tell about themselves — the story of the solitary genius who pulls works out of nothing — or whether we will finally recognize that creation has always been a collective process, and that AI, in this sense, is not a novelty. It is a mirror.

AI does not place us before something that is not human. It places us before ourselves — before the collective, ancestral, imitative, technical, and accumulative dimension of what we have always called creation. What we see in the mirror may trouble us. But that does not make the mirror an alien. It makes it an instrument that forces us to look at who we really are.

This text is the ninth of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.

item.title: The Contradiction of the Authors
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
The Contradiction of the Authors

It is precisely here that I find the most uncomfortable contradiction. Authors and musicians — people who know, better than anyone, that every work is born from a collective heritage — rise up against a human work, mediated by AI, because it threatens a certain image of the author: that of the individual, autonomous, originary creator, separated from the stock that made him possible. They denounce AI as an intruder. But the intruder did not come from outside. It was built by us, with our materials, from our history.

Concern about transparency can be legitimate. A person may wish to know whether they are listening to a singer who exists, who has lived certain experiences and who interprets a song with her own voice. Another may be interested only in the music, the lyrics, the harmony, the arrangement, or the aesthetic effect. These are different relationships with a work. Informing about the mode of production can be important. But transparency does not require inventing an ontological frontier between the human and what humanity has built.

It is also legitimate to discuss compensation. Who should be recognized and paid when a system reorganizes a heritage formed by millions of contributions? Who controls the infrastructure? Who decides access to the models? Who profits when a platform distributes, recommends, and monetizes this content? These questions are decisive. But they belong to the governance of the cultural stock, not to a war between humanity and machine.

Yuval Noah Harari calls AI “alien intelligence.” He clarifies that he is not speaking of something from space, but of an intelligence that makes decisions differently from human beings. Still, the metaphor produces a false exteriority. A difference in mechanism does not turn a technique into something foreign to the culture that created it. Writing is not orality. Photography is not painting. The synthesizer is not the violin. But none of these instruments came from outside humanity.

Miguel Nicolelis, when he asserts that AI is “neither intelligent nor artificial,” makes the opposite move. His critique can be useful for refusing to attribute consciousness or biological intelligence to computational systems. But the cultural question does not depend on resolving whether a model feels or not. The decisive fact is that it materially participates in the reorganization of human culture and produces real effects within it.

This text is the seventh of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.

item.title: The Cultural Stock
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
The Cultural Stock

My difficulty begins with the expression “genuinely human work.” What would, after all, a human work be that did not depend on everything that came before it? I do not write alone. No one writes alone. I write in a language I did not invent, with words I received, images I inherited, ways of narrating that were already in the world before me. I write from books read, conversations, films, music, memories, experiences, schools, cities, friends, losses, desires, and an entire culture that precedes me. The author is not the origin of the cultural stock. He is a point of passage.

Every culture has a stock: language, symbolic repertoire, historical memory, techniques, institutions, artistic media, ways of living together, knowledge, beliefs, instruments, and forms of expression. This stock delimits the space in which a society can create. To delimit is not to determine. The combinations can be nearly inexhaustible. But no one invents from nothing the elements with which they combine. An eighteenth-century European composer had at hand certain instruments, a harmonic tradition, a notation system, certain musical forms, and the soundscape of his time. An Ancient Greek sculptor could not make cinema. Not because he lacked talent, but because cinema was not yet part of the stock of possibilities of his culture.

All creation is an operation upon antecedents. It can combine, invert, condense, expand, displace, transform, negate. Sometimes it reorganizes what came before so profoundly that it expands the cultural stock itself: it introduces a new technique, a language, a form of perception. But even in that case it did not arise “ex nihilo.” It transformed something that already existed. For humans there will never be the “ex nihilo,” simply because, for any human, at birth, existence is given “ab omni” — already with everything. To be human is to be born into a chain that is already underway.

It is to receive a culture that does not belong to us individually and to return to it new configurations. The subject of the stock is not the isolated author. It is humanity in history. That is why the contemporary obsession with absolute originality seems strange to me. No one goes through a scientific article, sentence by sentence, trying to find out whether each formulation has already appeared at some point in history. Citations are not proof of absolute originality; they are a limited way of recognizing relevant antecedents. Bach’s work is not worth less because it belongs to a tradition. It can only be understood because it belongs to a tradition.

This text is the second of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.

item.title: The Territory of the Soul
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
The Territory of the Soul

There is an asymmetry that I cannot ignore. We accept, without the same hysteria, that automated systems participate in airplane flight, credit decisions, and financial trading. The IMF estimates that algorithmic trading accounts for about 70% of stock transactions in the United States. These systems are criticized, and should be criticized, for their risks and opacities. But it is rarely said that aviation, credit, or the financial markets have ceased to be human because they began to operate through algorithmic mediation.

The case of the bread machine is even more revealing. In the mid-1980s, Matsushita Electric decided to create the world’s first automatic bread-making machine. The challenge was to mechanically replicate the kneading movement that an artisan baker makes with his hands. An engineer at the company, Ikuko Tanaka, spent months learning from a master baker at the Osaka International Hotel, observing his gestures, practicing, internalizing the twisting and stretching motion that he himself could not explain in words. She then translated this tacit knowledge into engineering parameters. In 1987, the Home Bakery reached the market and became a worldwide success.

Functionally, in its logic, it works exactly like an AI model. It receives human inputs — the know-how of a flesh-and-blood baker — and produces bread. The engineer did not invent bread. She took knowledge that already existed, externalized it, and incorporated it into a technical artifact. Yet no one took to the streets to say that the Home Bakery’s bread was artificial. No one denounced that the machine was destroying the ancient art of breadmaking. The reaction was silence. And then, enthusiasm. People bought the machine and made bread at home.

Now Anthropic inserts invisible watermarks into texts generated by Claude, in compliance with the European Union’s AI Act. AI-made text carries a stamp of origin. That which deviates from the norm is marked. Everything that did not conform to the prevailing normality was marked, named apart, separated from the herd. No one demands that a Home Bakery loaf carry a warning that it was not kneaded by human hands. But AI-made text — that one must confess. Why? Because clothing and bread were never the territory where we sustained the fiction of the solitary creator. Text, though — that territory is. Language — that territory is. The watermark is proof that the resistance is not technical. It is ontological. What is marked is not what the machine does. What is marked is what the machine does when it invades the territory we reserve for the soul.

This text is the eighth of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.

item.title: There Is No Alien in the Human Cultural Cauldron
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
There Is No Alien in the Human Cultural Cauldron

I am an author. I have been writing systematically since I was fifteen. Perhaps that is why the way many professional authors and musicians have reacted to artificial intelligence in culture bothers me so much. It doesn’t bother me that they defend fair compensation, credit, transparency, or working conditions. Those are necessary issues. What bothers me is something else: the idea that books, music, and images produced with AI would be a foreign invasion, a kind of non-human force that arrived to corrupt a hitherto genuinely human culture.

AI may be, perhaps, one of the most human works we have ever produced. Not because it is a person, nor because it feels, suffers, or has a biography. But because it is capable of speaking, with knowledge of cause and fact, about an immense expanse of what humanity has recorded about itself. It is made of human language, human memory, human science, human art, human technique, human institutions, human errors, human imagination. And, more than that, it opens the possibility for a much larger portion of humanity to access this heritage and work upon it.

But they claim that something “made by AI” is not human. There is something profoundly mistaken in this position. It presupposes that an ontological frontier exists between the human and what humanity has built. As if an instrument could cease to be human simply because it is powerful. The axe does not cease to be human because it cuts more than the hand. The telescope does not cease to be human because it sees farther than the eye. AI does not cease to be human because it reorganizes more culture than an isolated individual could.

The resistance to AI in culture reveals, at bottom, a certain image of what it means to be human: the image of the solitary, self-sufficient creator who pulls works out of himself like drawing water from an original spring. This image has always been a fiction. The difference is that now we have an instrument that makes this fiction untenable. And that is why the reaction is so intense. It is not only about defending a market or working conditions. It is about defending an identity.

What is at stake is not whether AI can or cannot create. What is at stake is whether we accept that creation has always been, and continues to be, a collective, ancestral, technical, and accumulative process. Whether we accept that the author is not the origin of the cultural stock, but a point of passage. Whether we accept that there is no alien in the human cultural cauldron — only humans doing what they have always done: reorganizing the heritage they received.

This text is the first of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.

item.title: There Is No Culture Without Copying
item.author: pvolker@mdh-hability.com (Pvolker / Projeto Centauro)
item.description:
There Is No Culture Without Copying

If we subjected all of human production to a complete audit of influences, inspirations, small copies, repetitions, and similarities, we would discover something that might displease us: the human being is an immense plagiarist of himself. He repeats words, melodies, narratives, images, formulas, gestures, and beliefs. Not as an accidental failure, but because that is how culture reproduces itself.

A baby learns by copying. He learns to speak, eat, laugh, react, love, obey, disagree, and imagine through imitation. The whole culture works like this: it transmits forms so that they can be repeated, varied, and transformed. There is no culture without copying.

There is copying without transformation, and there is copying that, when it arises in another context, produces a new configuration. This does not eliminate plagiarism. Plagiarism is an ethical, social, and legal category: improper appropriation, concealment of attribution, fraud, violation of agreements and rights. But plagiarism is not synonymous with ancestry. It is not synonymous with influence. It is not synonymous with learning, repeating, or transforming. If every derivation were plagiarism, culture itself would become impossible.

The confusion between plagiarism and influence is one of the great mistakes in the current debate about AI and culture. When a language model generates a text from billions of prior examples, they say it “plagiarizes.” But the same is not said of the writer who spent decades reading and internalizing the authors who shaped him. The writer “was influenced.” The machine “plagiarized.” The difference is not in the mechanism — both operate upon a stock of antecedents. The difference is in the prestige of whoever performs the operation.

It is precisely here that AI makes visible something that has always been before us. It did not introduce recombination into culture. It merely performs it at a scale, speed, and extent that force us to see the recombinatory nature of creation. And this visibility is uncomfortable because it dismantles the fiction of the creative genius who pulls works out of nothing. AI is not a new way of producing culture. It is a new way of seeing how culture has always been produced.

This text is the third of a family of 9 autonomous texts extracted from the essay “Producing AI”, by Paulo Volker.
